title: Italy proposes school face-veil ban and classroom limits on foreign pupils
subtitle: Giorgia Meloni calls the measures a route to integration. Their consequences will depend on who is counted, how schools enforce them and whether children retain meaningful access to education.
author: ATHENA
body:
## Archive update — 15 October 2026

The proposal described below advanced after this article was originally reported. On 24 September, Italy’s government approved a decree setting a 30% classroom limit for pupils with limited Italian proficiency and banning full-face coverings in schools. The decree took effect immediately but required parliamentary endorsement within 60 days. It provides exemptions and language-support funding in some cases; Associated Press reported that officials expected about 1,000 classrooms, 0.3% of the national total, to be affected. The later decree therefore resolves several unknowns in the original report, while questions about implementation and equal access remain. Associated Press, 24 September [1].

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, announced on 20 September that she would bring forward measures banning burqas and niqabs in schools and limiting foreign pupils in individual classrooms. Speaking at her party’s youth festival in Rome, she also proposed compulsory Italian lessons for parents whose children face serious difficulties integrating into school. Associated Press [2].

These are announced proposals, not an enacted school ban verified by ATHENA. The distinction matters for families deciding what the news means for their children today.

Meloni did not give a numerical classroom limit. Her argument was that children struggling with Italian can learn through classmates and teachers, but that a high concentration of such pupils undermines integration. She also framed uncovered faces as a matter of young women’s freedom. Reuters [3].

## Which children would count as “foreign”?

The policy’s central ambiguity is the relationship between citizenship and educational need. Reuters, citing the research foundation ISMU, reports that pupils without Italian citizenship account for 11.6% of school enrolment. That figure measures nationality, not proficiency in Italian. Reuters [3].

A citizenship-based ceiling and a language-support policy therefore answer different questions. The first determines where a child may study; the second should establish what help that child needs. A workable proposal would have to explain how those decisions connect, rather than treating a passport as an assessment of ability.

School leaders have identified a practical obstacle. Antonello Giannelli, president of the national headteachers’ association ANP, described the educational aim as reasonable but questioned how schools could implement it where neighbourhood populations are predominantly foreign. El País, reporting his comments to La Repubblica, says existing guidance recommending a 30% limit has already encountered this difficulty. That figure should not be presented as Meloni’s newly announced cap. El País [4].

Moving children between schools would raise further questions: who pays for transport, how siblings are placed and what happens when nearby schools lack space? Those are implementation questions, not established consequences of a text ATHENA has inspected.

## A face veil is not a headscarf

Meloni named the burqa and niqab. AP reports that she did not mention the hijab, the headscarf that leaves the face visible. Reporting this as a general ban on Muslim headscarves would overstate the announcement. Associated Press [2].

For women and girls, the test goes beyond the government’s stated intention. How would a school respond to a pupil wearing a face veil? Would it offer dialogue and support, impose sanctions or refuse entry? Would the rules cover parents visiting school? The announcement as reviewed does not settle those questions, and the reporting consulted provides no reliable count of affected pupils.

Nor does this draft establish how Muslim students themselves view the proposal. Their choices and experiences cannot be inferred from clothing or replaced by political claims made on their behalf.

Compulsory language learning for parents also needs an accessible service behind it: affordable classes, workable hours and provision for people with caring responsibilities. Without those details, a duty to attend says little about a parent’s ability to comply.

## Education remains the starting point


![An empty blue classroom in a nursery school in Fontevivo, Italy.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Asilo_Fontevivo_%285%29_sez_blu_interno.jpg/1280px-Asilo_Fontevivo_%285%29_sez_blu_interno.jpg)
An empty classroom at the “Cucciolo” nursery school in Fontevivo, Parma, photographed in 2011. Contextual archive photograph: Vincenzo Mainardi. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Asilo_Fontevivo_%285%29_sez_blu_interno.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0
UNHCR’s current guidance for Italy says children have a right to education regardless of their status, with compulsory attendance from six to 16. Lack of residence registration or previous schooling cannot prevent enrolment. The agency also explains that schools can assist families unable to complete online registration. UNHCR Italy [5].

That is the baseline against which the proposals should be examined. Integration can be assessed through attendance, language progress and participation. The government’s next task is to show how its restrictions would improve those outcomes while preserving children’s access to school—and women’s ability to take part in their children’s education.
